messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh is a kind man with a deeply lined face, a man who has spent his seventy-two years dedicated to helping others navigate the aftermath of chaos. For four decades, his work as a refugee aid worker had been his calling, a source of immense purpose. That purpose was shattered six months ago on a dusty road outside a displacement camp. He had been in the lead vehicle of a small convoy, a routine supply run he’d made a hundred times. He remembers the bright, almost peaceful morning light. The memory doesn't come back as a coherent story, but as a series of silent, searing images: the glint of sunlight off something metallic by the roadside, the sudden bloom of orange and black smoke, the world turning upside down in a storm of glass and twisted metal. When the memories come, they are mostly these pictures, a slideshow of the worst moment of his life. Sometimes, though, the sound breaks through the silence—not the explosion itself, but the high-pitched, electronic whine that filled his ears in the moments just after, a sound he now hears when the house is too quiet. He often tells his wife that it feels utterly unreal, like a movie he once saw. It’s a story so extreme he finds it hard to believe it actually happened to him.

In the weeks that followed, Minh returned home to the US, but he never truly left that road. He began to see danger everywhere. A car backfiring on his street sends him to the floor, heart hammering against his ribs. The sharp slam of a filing cabinet at the aid center where he now works makes him flinch so violently that his colleagues have learned to close doors softly around him. He is constantly on guard, his body rigid with a watchfulness that never subsides. He scans every room he enters, notes every exit, assesses every person who walks past the office window. This unrelenting vigilance has shrunk his world to two locations: his small apartment and his office cubicle. These are the only places he feels a semblance of safety, the only zones where the threat feels manageable.

To cope, Minh has systematically dismantled his own life. He no longer drives. The simple act of sitting in a vehicle, passenger or driver, brings the images and the ringing in his ears flooding back with unbearable intensity. He gave up his senior field position, the part of his job he loved most, and now confines himself to administrative tasks. This has created a rift with his old team, a quiet distance that pains him. He also avoids any form of conflict. At a recent staff meeting, a junior colleague openly questioned his proposed budget. Instead of defending his work, Minh felt a surge of pure panic, the same helpless terror from the attack, and immediately conceded. He had come to believe that any disagreement, no matter how small, was a precursor to violence. The most punishing strategy, however, is the one that happens inside his own mind. He was the one who approved the convoy’s route that morning. He circles this fact for hours every day, a private, relentless self-prosecution. He repeatedly blames himself for what happened, convinced that if he had been more careful, more vigilant, his colleagues would still be alive.

It was his wife, Lan, who finally insisted he seek help. She found him one evening standing motionless in their living room, staring at the television long after it had been turned off, his body trembling after a motorcycle roared past their window. She took his hand and said his name three times before he seemed to hear her. He is terrified that the damage is permanent, that the calm, capable man he once was is gone forever. His greatest fear is that he will never escape the endless loop of blame and the constant feeling of being hunted. Yet, a small part of him hopes that he might one day be able to sit in a park with his wife without scanning the rooftops, or drive to the grocery store without the world outside the windshield feeling like a mortal threat.
